analysis.investment_thesis: Crizac is a genuinely high-quality, debt-free student recruitment business with exceptional ROCE (48%) and a pristine balance sheet, but the price at 20.8x P/E and 17.6x EV/EBITDA embeds continued hypergrowth assumptions precisely when its core markets — Canada, UK, Australia — are actively throttling international student inflows. The regulatory cycle has turned; the stock price has not adjusted to reflect it.
key_strengths: Zero debt + INR 89 Cr cash with 4/4 years of positive operating cash flow — an operationally pristine balance sheet for a services business
Exceptional capital efficiency: ROCE of 48% with near-zero capex requirements in normal years (capex INR 1 Cr in FY25), producing INR 188 Cr FCF
Four-year revenue CAGR of 66% with operating leverage intact — EBITDA margins expanded from ~24% to ~28% as scale accrued
key_risks: Existential regulatory risk: Canada (likely top revenue source) imposed international student permit caps in Jan 2024, renewed in 2025; UK, Australia, and NZ have each tightened dependent/student visa rules — the company's entire addressable market is shrinking by government fiat

Other income of INR 35–53 Cr annually represents ~23–46% of net profit in recent years — strip it out and core operating profitability is materially overstated; this treasury/non-operating cushion will shrink as policy risk bites revenues
Promoter holding of 79.94% leaves a thin public float (~20%), meaning any institutional exit or earnings disappointment will face poor liquidity on the way down
red_flags: Recent IPO vintage (2024 listing) — priced during peak enthusiasm for study-abroad sector, now facing a structural policy reversal in its primary markets
INR 119 Cr capex spike in FY24 from a historically near-zero capex business is unexplained — unusual for an asset-light services firm and warrants scrutiny on capital deployment discipline
Forward P/E of 16x implies ~30% earnings growth consensus — this is optimistic given Canada's student permit volume has already fallen 35%+ year-over-year
analysis.detailed_analysis: The surface numbers on Crizac are genuinely impressive: 66% revenue CAGR, 48% ROCE, zero debt, and a FCF yield of approximately 4.7% (INR 188 Cr FCF / INR 4,028 Cr market cap). A first-level observer sees a compounding machine. But second-level thinking demands we ask: what does the price already assume, and what external shocks could invalidate those assumptions? The answer to the second question is deeply uncomfortable. The business model is a direct pass-through of Indian student demand for foreign higher education — specifically in Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, and NZ. Every one of those five markets has enacted material restrictions on international student inflows in 2023–2025. Canada, which absorbs a disproportionate share of Indian student outflows, cut annual study permits by 35%+ and extended the cap through 2025. That is not a cyclical wobble — it is a structural policy reversal that directly compresses Crizac's addressable volume.
